translationRepairs: He was posthumously enfeoffed as Vice Director of the Central Secretariat.
He was posthumously granted the title of Vice Director of the Central Secretariat.
追贈中書侍郎 is a posthumous grant of office; enfeoffment (封) is not in the Chinese, and the proposed wording matches the sense.
Duke Xu of Ancheng, son of Wuji, and Duke Lingxiu of Linru, son of Chang, were equally lavish; with Zhanzhi they competed in cuisine, furnishings, dress, and equipage.
He Xu, Duke of Ancheng, son of Wuji, and Meng Lingxiu, Duke of Linru, son of Chang, were equally lavish; with Zhanzhi they competed in cuisine, furnishings, dress, and equipage.
安成公何勖 and 臨汝公孟靈休 name He Xu and Meng Lingxiu; ‘Duke Xu’ and ‘Duke Lingxiu’ wrongly treat personal names as surnames/titles.
Xu rose to Palace Attendant and was posthumously given the temple name Duke of Dissipation.
Xu rose to Palace Attendant and was posthumously given the posthumous name Duke of Dissipation.
追諡荒公 awards a posthumous name (諡); temple name (廟號) is a different category and is not present here.
Lingxiu was a master of pitch-pot and rose to Director of the Secretariat.
Lingxiu was a master of the board game tanqi and rose to Director of the Secretariat.
彈棋 is the board game tanqi; pitch-pot is 投壺 and is not the game named here.
He had three sons: Yuzhi and Qianzhi were killed by Liu Shao.
Of his three sons, Yuzhi and Qianzhi were killed by Liu Shao.
三子：聿之、謙之，為元凶所殺 names only two of the three sons as killed; the colon-list English wrongly implies the roster is complete in this sentence, while 恆之 follows in s0132.
Dan's consort was Xu Zhanzhi's daughter; Shuo's consort was his sister.
Dan's consort was Xu Zhanzhi's daughter; Shuo's consort was Xu Zhanzhi's sister.
鑠妃即湛妹 makes Shuo’s consort Zhanzhi’s sister; ‘his sister’ could be read as Dan’s or Shuo’s sister, so naming Xu Zhanzhi removes the ambiguity.
